Layer.Name: marine_pathogen:chesbay_vibrio_vulnificus
Layer.Title: Chesapeake Bay Probability of Vibrio Vulnificus
Layer.Abstract: This nowCOAST map service provides maps of NOAA/NOS' latest forecast guidance for the probability of occurrence of Vibrio vulnificus (Vv), a marine pathogen which can cause illness and hospitalization. The Vv model predicts the probability of Vv occurrence based on nowcasts and forecast guidance of water temperature and salinity from the 0000 UTC forecast cycle of the NOS Chesapeake Bay Operational Forecast System (CBOFS). The CBOFS temperature and salinity predictions are averaged over a 24-hour period and over the top 1 meter to provide averages centered around 0600 UTC. This is accomplished by using the hourly nowcasts valid from 1900 UTC to 2300 UTC from the previous day and the hourly forecast guidance valid at forecast projections 0- to 18-hr (i.e. valid for hours 0000 to 1800 UTC) of the present day. These 24-hour averages of temperature and salinity for the present day are then used by the Vv model to generate the Day 1 predictions. CBOFS' hourly guidance for forecast projections 19- to 42-hr are used to calculate average temperatures and salinities centered at the 30-hr forecast projection. These averages are used by the Vv model to generate its Day 2 predictions. Due to a bias in CBOFS' salinity predictions, the salinity predictions are automatically corrected based on near-real-time observations from several buoys in the bay before the predictions are used by the Vv model.

Layer.Name: satellite:global_longwave_imagery_mosaic
Layer.Title: Global Satellite Longwave Imagery
Layer.Abstract: The NOAA/NESDIS Global Mosaic of Geostationary Satellite Imagery (GMGSI) longwave, thermal infrared band (~12.0 μm), has an hourly update frequency, approximately 3 km spatial resolution, the data latency is two to three hours and depicts cloud cover and land/sea temperature patterns. The channel is used in many baseline products, such as Fire Detection, Volcanic Ash Detection, and Derived Motion Wind Vector.

Layer.Name: sea_surface_temperature:global_sea_surface_temperature
Layer.Title: NOAA GFS Sea Surface Temperature
Layer.Abstract: The NWS Global SST Analysis is generated by the Near-Surface Sea Temperature (NSST) Scheme of the NWS/NCEP Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) and the Global Forecast System (GFS). The analysis provides estimates of surface water temperatures for the world oceans, seas (e.g. Black Sea) and the Great Lakes. The NSST analysis is specifically the GDAS 1200 UTC NSST “foundation temperature” interpolated to the 1/12 degrees resolution grid of the decommissioned NWS Real-Time High Resolution SST Analysis. The NSST global analysis is generated by NCEP once per day and is considered operational.

Layer.Name: satellite:global_shortwave_imagery_mosaic
Layer.Title: Global Satellite Shortwave Imagery
Layer.Abstract: The NOAA/NESDIS Global Mosaic of Geostationary Satellite Imagery (GMGSI) shortwave, mid-infrared band (~3.8 μm), has an hourly update frequency, approximately 3 km spatial resolution, and can be used to identify fog and low clouds at night, identify fire hot spots, detect volcanic ash, estimate sea-surface temperatures, and discriminate between ice crystal sizes during the day. Low-level atmospheric vector winds can be estimated with this band, and the band can be used to study urban heat islands.

Layer.Name: satellite:global_visible_imagery_mosaic
Layer.Title: Global Satellite Visible Imagery
Layer.Abstract: The NOAA/NESDIS Global Mosaic of Geostationary Satellite Imagery (GMGSI) visible band (~0.6 μm), has an hourly update frequency, approximately 3 km spatial resolution, the data latency is two to three hours, and provides detection and analysis of clouds and weather systems during daytime. Half-kilometer resolution allows detection of boundaries and small clouds, especially useful in mesoscale sectors for rapidly changing phenomena.

Layer.Name: satellite:global_water_vapor_imagery_mosaic
Layer.Title: Global Satellite Water Vapor Imagery
Layer.Abstract: The NOAA/NESDIS Global Mosaic of Geostationary Satellite Imagery (GMGSI) water vapor band (~6.7 µm), has an hourly update frequency, approximately 3 km spatial resolution, the data latency is two to three hours, and indicates the amount of water vapor contained in the mid to upper levels of the troposphere, with the darker grays indicating drier air and the brighter grays/whites indicating more saturated air. The upper-level water vapor band is used for tracking upper-tropospheric winds, identifying jet streams, forecasting hurricane track and mid-latitude storm motion, monitoring severe weather potential, estimating upper/mid-level moisture and identifying regions where the potential for turbulence exists.

Layer.Name: satellite:goes_longwave_imagery
Layer.Title: GOES East & West Satellite Longwave Imagery
Layer.Abstract: NOAA/NASA Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) Longwave Infrared Band 14 (11.2 μm), has a 5 min update frequency and a 2 km spatial resolution. Data from the 11.2 μm channel is used in many Baseline Products, such as Fire Detection, Volcanic Ash Detection, Derived Motion Wind Vectors, Legacy Atmospheric Profiles including Precipitable Water, Cloud Top Properties, Aerosol Detection and Land Surface Temperature. This composite longwave imagery contains GOES-19 (East) and GOES-18 (West) from GOES Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) Level 1b (L1b), L1b products are calibrated and, where applicable, geographically corrected.

Layer.Name: satellite:goes_shortwave_imagery
Layer.Title: GOES East & West Satellite Shortwave Imagery
Layer.Abstract: NOAA/NASA Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) Shortwave Band 7 (3.9 μm), has a 5 min update frequency, 2 km spatial resolution, and can be used to identify fog and low clouds at night, identify fire hot spots, detect volcanic ash, estimate sea-surface temperatures, and discriminate between ice crystal sizes during the day. Low-level atmospheric vector winds can be estimated with this band, and the band can be used to study urban heat islands. The 3.9 μm is unique among ABI bands because it senses both emitted terrestrial radiation as well as significant reflected solar radiation during the day. This composite shortwave imagery contains GOES-19 (East) and GOES-18 (West) from GOES Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) Level 1b (L1b), L1b products are calibrated and, where applicable, geographically corrected.

Layer.Name: satellite:goes_snow_ice_imagery
Layer.Title: GOES East & West Satellite Snow/Ice Imagery
Layer.Abstract: NOAA/NASA Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) Snow/Ice Band 5 (1.61 μm), has a 5 min update frequency, 1 km spatial resolution, and takes advantage of the difference between the refraction components of water and ice at 1.61 μm. Liquid water clouds are bright in this channel; ice clouds are darker because ice absorbs (rather than reflects) radiation at 1.61 μm. Thus you can infer cloud phase: compare at right the darker region of the cirrus anvil to the more reflective water-based cumulus clouds to the right of the storm. Land/water contrast is great at 1.61 μm (lakes are readily apparent in the image) and shadows can be particularly striking. Fires can also be detected at night using this band. This composite snow/ice imagery contains GOES-19 (East) and GOES-18 (West) from GOES Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) Level 1b (L1b), L1b products are calibrated and, where applicable, geographically corrected.

Layer.Name: satellite:goes_visible_imagery
Layer.Title: GOES East & West Satellite Visible Imagery
Layer.Abstract: NOAA/NASA Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) Visible Band 2 (0.64 μm), has a 5 min update frequency, 0.5 km spatial resolution, and provides detection and analysis of clouds and weather systems during daytime. Half-kilometer resolution allows detection of boundaries and small clouds, especially useful in mesoscale sectors for rapidly changing phenomena. Limitation Pixel reflectance in this band can exceed 100% over thick clouds for a large solar zenith angle because of contributions to reflectance from scattering within the cloud. This composite visible imagery contains GOES-19 (East) and GOES-18 (West) from GOES Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) Level 1b (L1b), L1b products are calibrated and, where applicable, geographically corrected.

Layer.Name: satellite:goes_water_vapor_imagery
Layer.Title: GOES East & West Satellite Water Vapor Imagery
Layer.Abstract: NOAA/NASA Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) Upper-Level Water Vapor Band 8 (6.2 μm), has a 5 min update frequency, 2 km spatial resolution, and is one of three water vapor bands on the ABI, and is used for tracking upper-tropospheric winds, identifying jet streams, forecasting hurricane track and mid-latitude storm motion, monitoring severe weather potential, estimating upper/mid-level moisture (for legacy vertical moisture profiles) and identifying regions where the potential for turbulence exists. Further, it can be used to validate numerical model initialization and warming/cooling with time can reveal vertical motions at mid and upper levels. Primary application atmospheric feature identification (jet streams, troughs/ridges, signatures of potential turbulence).This composite water vapor imagery contains GOES-19 (East) and GOES-18 (West) from GOES Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) Level 1b (L1b), L1b products are calibrated and, where applicable, geographically corrected.

Layer.Name: geopotential:grav2022
Layer.Title: Bouguer Gravity (GRAV2022)
Layer.Abstract: GRAV2022 provides a height adjustment for land topography with respect to the Earth’s surface (Bouguer anomaly) and is consistent with the geoid (GEOID2022) dataset. The terrestrial adjustment layer provides the surface gravity value at a user’s specified location and can be used in local high-accuracy application, such as geodetic leveling corrections and adjusting the GMSL for lakes or sections of river at a given topography. Corrections to the GMSL using the GRAV2022 layer are called “dynamic heights”. For more information and interpolation tools, please refer to: https://beta.ngs.noaa.gov/NAPGD2022 and https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/474f5934f5ff468bb77a1a16f10aa578/page/GRAV2022-(RBA). The NAPGD2022 models shown here are beta and intended for informational purposes only. This is not an official NGS product and is subject to change. The NAPGD2022 layers provided on nowCOAST are provided by NOAA's NGS. For an official product and latest version of tools available, please visit https://www.ngs.noaa.gov/ Source: NOAA NOS/NGS.

Layer.Name: tropical_storm_surge:inundation
Layer.Title: Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map
Layer.Abstract: The Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map layer depicts the risk associated with coastal flooding from storm surge associated with tropical cyclones. The map depicts the geographical areas where inundation from storm surge could occur along with the heights, above ground, that water could reach in those areas. These potential heights are represented with different colors based on water level: 1) Greater than 1 foot above ground (blue), 2) Greater than 3 feet above ground (yellow), 3) Greater than 6 feet above ground (orange), and 4) Greater than 9 feet above ground (red). Once issued, the Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map will be updated by NHC every six hours alongside each new Forecast Advisory for the associated tropical cyclone. NHC inundation maps are available approximately 60 to 90 minutes following the release of the associated NHC Forecast Advisory, nowCOAST will acquire it and update this layer approximately 70 minutes after the associated Forecast Advisory is released.

Layer.Name: lightning_detection:ldn_lightning_strike_density
Layer.Title: Lightning Strike Density Data
Layer.Abstract: The Lightning Strike Density maps highlight the location of lightning cores and trends of increasing and decreasing activity. The maps depict the density of lightning strikes, cloud-to-ground strikes, cloud-to-ground flash information and survey level cloud lightning information during a 15-minute time period at an 8 x 8 km (5 x 5 mile) horizontal resolution observed by ground-based lightning detection networks. These networks include the U.S. National Lightning Detection Network (NLDN) and the Global Lightning Detection Network (GLD360). The lightning strike density maps cover the geographic area from 25 degrees South to 80 degrees North latitude and from 110 degrees East to 0 degrees West longitude. The map units are the number of strikes per square km per minute multiplied by a scaling factor of 10^3. The strike density is color coded using a color scheme which allows the data to be easily seen when overlaid on weather satellite imagery and to distinguish areas of low- and high- density values. The maps are updated approximately every 15 minutes. The lightning strike density data is obtained from the NWS/NCEP/Ocean Prediction Center. The data is considered a derived product or Level 5 product (NOAA-generated products using lightning data as input but not displaying the contractor (Vaisala) transmitted provided lightning data) and is appropriate for public distribution. The purpose of this product is to provide mariners and others with enhanced awareness of developing and transitory thunderstorm activity to give users the ability to determine whether a cloud system is producing lightning and if that activity is increasing or decreasing.

Layer.Name: boundaries:military_boundaries
Layer.Title: Working Military Areas
Layer.Abstract: This nowCOAST map service provides a map depicting the boundaries of U.S. Dept. of Defense (DOD) working military areas of the United States. Presently, only the boundaries of the VACAPES and Cherry Point Range Complex Operating Areas (OPAREA) in the Mid-Atlantic Region are provided along with associated Special Use Airspace (SUA) in Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia, and North Carolina. The military working areas include airspace, seaspace, and undersea space. These areas are used by the U.S. DOD for training and testing purposes.

Layer.Name: sea_surface_temperature:nasa_sport_sea_surface_temperature
Layer.Title: NASA SPoRT Sea Surface Temperature
Layer.Abstract: The NASA/SPoRT Sea Surface Temperature (SST) composite provides satellite-retrieval estimates of surface water temperatures for nearly the entire globe. The analysis is a 7-day weighted composite of the following data and analyses: 1) SST retrieval by VIIRS on S-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 satellites and 2) SST retrieval by AVHRR on MetOp-B and MetOp-C satellites. Where no satellite retrieval has occurred over the last 7 days the NOAA/NESDIS daily global blended GOES/POES SST Analysis and the United Kingdom Meteorological Office daily Operational Sea Surface Temperature and Ice Analysis (OSTIA) system are used to fill gaps. However, for inland lakes the GOES/POES SST analysis is not available. The SPoRT SST is calculated on a 2-km (1.1 nm) grid. The 7-day composite is generated twice daily and valid for the periods 0000-1159 UTC and 1200-2359 UTC. The composite is not 24 x 7 operationally supported by NASA, so it should be considered a 'Data of Opportunity'.

Layer.Name: s100:s100_interoperable_coverage
Layer.Title: S-100 Interoperable Coverage
Layer.Abstract: This S-100 interoperable coverage service identifies and visualizes areas where multiple S-100 products overlap, in accordance with S-98 interoperability principles. The service provides combined coverage for NOAA Bathymetric Surface data (S-102) and Water Level data (S-104), highlighting regions where both products are available for integrated use. The S-100 products are referenced to chart datum (MLLW) and are intended to support navigation, Water Level Adjustment, and decision-making in Electronic Chart Display and Information System (ECDIS) and Portable Pilot Unit (PPU) systems. By exposing overlapping product extents, this service enables systems and users to determine where consistent, multi-source S-100 data coverage exists for enhanced situational awareness and interoperability. Data Source: NOS/OCS

Layer.Name: s100:s102_coverage
Layer.Title: S-102 Coverage
Layer.Abstract: This S-100 product coverage service provides maps of the present geographic coverage of NOAA’s Bathymetric Surfaces (S-102). S-102 is a data encoding specification that is part of the S-100 Universal Hydrographic Data Model, an international standard for hydrographic data. This collection of S-102 HDF5 datasets contains bathymetric surfaces on chart datum (MLLW or a local datum) from NOAA/NOS/OCS National Bathymetric Source, which creates and maintains high-resolution bathymetry composed of the best available data for various U.S. coastal and offshore waters and the Great Lakes. Primary sources of bathymetry include NOAA and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers hydrographic surveys and topographic bathymetric lidar data with a horizontal resolution of 4 meters. Data submitted through the NOAA Office of Coast Survey’s external source data process are also included, with gaps in deep water filled through Global Multi-Resolution Topography, a merged model of bathymetry. S-102 files are arranged in a tiling and naming scheme corresponding to the NOAA's Navigation Tile Scheme for Navigational Approach (Band 4), Harbor Navigation (Band 5), and Berthing Navigation (Band 6) coverage. For more information and data access visit https://registry.opendata.aws/noaa-s102/. Data Source: NOS/OCS

Layer.Name: s100:s104_coverage
Layer.Title: S-104 Coverage
Layer.Abstract: This S-100 product coverage service provides maps of the present geographic coverage of NOAA’s Water Level Information for Surface Navigation (S-104) and describes the status of S-104 products. S-104 is a data encoding specification that is part of the S-100 Universal Hydrographic Data Model, an international standard for hydrographic data. For S-104, the maps depict the areas where forecast guidance of water level data from the Global 2D Surge and Tide Operational Forecast System (STOFS-2D-Global) are available in S-104 HDF5 file format at a 200 meter resolution on chart datum MLLW. S-104 files are arranged in a tiling and naming scheme corresponding to the NOAA's Navigation Tile Scheme. For more information and data access visit https://registry.opendata.aws/noaa-s104/. Data Source: NOS/OCS

Layer.Name: s100:s111_coverage
Layer.Title: S-111 Coverage
Layer.Abstract: This S-100 product coverage service provides maps of the present geographic coverage of NOAA’s Surface Currents (S-111) Edition 1.0.1. S-111 is a data encoding specification that is part of the S-100 Universal Hydrographic Data Model, an international standard for hydrographic data. For S-111, the maps depict the geographic areas where forecast guidance of surface water currents are available from NOAA’s National Ocean Service (NOS) coastal and Great Lakes operational oceanographic forecast modeling systems and NOAA’s National Weather Service (NWS) Global Real-Time Operational Forecast Modeling System (GRTOFS) in S-111 HDF5 file format. S-111 files are arranged in a tiling and naming scheme corresponding to the NOAA's Navigation Tile Scheme for Navigational Approach (Band 4) and General Navigation (Band 2) coverage. For more information and data access visit https://registry.opendata.aws/noaa-s111/. Data Source: NOS/OCS

Layer.Name: sfbofs:sfbofs_sfc_currents
Layer.Title: San Francisco Bay Surface Water Currents
Layer.Abstract: Latest forecast guidance of water currents at 4.5m from NOAA Operational Oceanographic Forecast Modeling Systems for oceans, coastal ocean and Great Lakes. Data Source: NOS and NWS/NCEP

Layer.Name: geopotential:sgeoid2022
Layer.Title: Geoid Undulation (SGEOID2022)
Layer.Abstract: GEOID2022 provides a height relationship between the North American Pacific Datum of 2022 (NAPGD2022) and the ellipsoid heights determined with GPS (Geodetic Reference System 1980, GRS80). GEOID2022 layers include the geoid heights related to the gravity field. For more information and interpolation tools, please refer to: https://beta.ngs.noaa.gov/NAPGD2022 and https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/474f5934f5ff468bb77a1a16f10aa578/page/GEOID2022. The NAPGD2022 models shown here are beta and intended for informational purposes only. This is not an official NGS product and is subject to change. The NAPGD2022 layers provided on nowCOAST are provided by NOAA's NGS. For an official product and latest version of tools available, please visit https://www.ngs.noaa.gov/ Source: NOAA NOS/NGS.

Layer.Name: boundaries:ss_ww_communication_points
Layer.Title: NWS Storm Surge Watch/Warning Communication Points
Layer.Abstract: NWS uses fixed Storm Surge Communication Points, similar to the tropical cyclone watch/warning breakpoints, to convey the approximate lateral extent of coastal areas at risk for life-threatening storm surge in its products. The NWS Storm Surge Watch/Warning Communication Points include the tropical cyclone warning breakpoints which also serve as surge communication points, along with additional surge communication points. Source: Modified NWS/NHC Text

Layer.Name: stofs2d:stofs2d_cwl_max_contours
Layer.Title: STOFS-2D-Global Maximum Combined Water Level Contours
Layer.Abstract: Global Surge and Tide Operational Forecast System (STOFS-2D-Global) maximum combined tides and surge water level (CWL) elevation field in local mean sea level (m, LMSL) contoured across the entire forecast cycle. The model forecast run cycles are (00Z, 06Z, 12Z, 18Z) daily. Source: NOS/OCS

Layer.Name: stofs3d:stofs3d_atlc_water_disturbance
Layer.Title: STOFS-3D-Atlantic Water Level Disturbance
Layer.Abstract: Latest model forecast guidance of maximum water level for regions with initial water depth below zero xGEOID20b (e.g. usually water) and maximum total water depth above the ground for regions with initial water depth above zero xGEOID20b (e.g. usually dry land) for the next 96 hours from NOS Surge and Tide Operational Forecast System-3D-Atlantic (STOFS-3D-Atlantic) from the combination of freshwater and coastal flooding. Data Source: NOS/OCS

Layer.Name: tbofs:tbofs_sfc_currents
Layer.Title: Tampa Bay Surface Water Currents
Layer.Abstract: Latest forecast guidance of water currents at 4.5m from NOAA Operational Oceanographic Forecast Modeling Systems for oceans, coastal ocean and Great Lakes. Data Source: NOS and NWS/NCEP

Layer.Name: boundaries:tc_ww_breakpoints
Layer.Title: NWS Tropical Cyclone Watch/Warning Breakpoints
Layer.Abstract: A NWS tropical cyclone breakpoint is defined as an agreed upon coastal location that can be chosen as one of two specific endpoints or designated places between which a tropical storm/hurricane watch/warning is in effect. The NWS designates the fixed locations along the U.S. East, Gulf, and California coasts, Puerto Rico, and Hawaii. Individual countries across the Caribbean, Central America, and South America provide coastal locations for their areas of responsibility to the NWS for the National Hurricane Center's use in tropical cyclone advisories when watches/warnings are issued by international partners. The National Hurricane Center maintains a list of pre-arranged breakpoints for the U.S. Atlantic and Gulf coasts, Mexico, Cuba and the Bahamas. Other sites are unofficial and sites not on the list can be selected if conditions warrant.

Layer.Name: tropical_storm_surge:tidalmask
Layer.Title: Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map with Intertidal Zone
Layer.Abstract: The Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map with Intertidal Zone layer depicts the risk associated with coastal flooding from storm surge associated with tropical cyclones. The map depicts the geographical areas where inundation from storm surge could occur along with the heights, above ground, that water could reach in those areas. These potential heights are represented with different colors based on water level: 1) Greater than 1 foot above ground (blue), 2) Greater than 3 feet above ground (yellow), 3) Greater than 6 feet above ground (orange), 4) Greater than 9 feet above ground (red), mask identifying Intertidal Zone/Estuarine Wetland areas (gray), and Levee Areas (black)

Layer.Name: vertical_land_motion:vlm_acceleration
Layer.Title: Average Annual Acceleration
Layer.Abstract: Average annual acceleration (mm/yr^2) for the U.S. East Coast are based on Vertical Land Motion data for the period from March 2017 to May 2023. VLM is the gradual or sudden upward or downward motion of the Earth’s surface as a result of natural or anthropogenic activities. The VLM data were estimated using high-accuracy Interferometric-Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) data.

Layer.Name: alerts:watches_warnings_advisories
Layer.Title: NWS Latest Watches, Warnings, Advisories, and Special Statements
Layer.Abstract: This nowCOAST map service provides maps depicting the geographic coverage of the latest NOAA/National Weather Service (NWS) Watches, Warnings, Advisories, and Statements for long-duration hazardous conditions. The colors used to identify the different watches, advisories, warnings, and special statements are the same colors used by the NWS on their map at http://www.weather.gov. The map service is updated approximately every 2 minutes.
